rows: Rational Numbers — The Number Line Sprint

{"schemaVersion":"lesson-plan.v1","title":"Rational Numbers — The Number Line Sprint","learningObjectives":["Define rational numbers and identify them on a number line","Apply closure, commutative and associative properties to rational numbers","Find rational numbers between two given rationals","Represent real-life quantities (temperature, bank balance) as rationals"],"successCriteria":["Students can classify numbers as rational/irrational with reasons","Students can order four rational numbers from least to greatest","Students can insert 3 rational numbers between 1/4 and 1/2"],"materials":["Number line printouts","Fraction cards set A–D","Whiteboard markers","Classwork notebook"],"stages":[{"stage":"ENGAGE","durationMinutes":8,"title":"The Thermometer Hook","teacherScript":"Ask: 'Yesterday Chennai was 38°C, today it dropped 3 degrees, and my bank app shows −₹1,275.50. What kind of numbers are these?' Collect answers on the board. Introduce the term 'rational number' — any number expressible as p/q, q ≠ 0.","analogy":"A rational number is like a pizza promise: you can always describe your share as a fraction of the whole — even if the pizza is debt (negative)!","boardWork":["Draw a giant number line from -3 to +3","Place -1/2, 3/4, -2.25 on it with student volunteers"],"workedExamples":[],"questions":[{"q":"Is 0 a rational number? Why?","expected":"Yes — 0 = 0/1, denominator non-zero."},{"q":"Can -5 be written as p/q?","expected":"Yes, -5 = -5/1."}],"differentiation":"Pair weaker readers with picture cards first; let advanced students challenge with π and √2."},{"stage":"EXPLORE","durationMinutes":10,"title":"Between Two Numbers","teacherScript":"Groups get cards 1/4 and 1/2. Challenge: 'Find a number that lives between them.' Then find another. Then another. Guide discovery that infinitely many rationals exist between any two.","analogy":"Numbers are like houses on a street — between any two houses you can always build another house.","boardWork":["Show 1/4 = 0.25 and 1/2 = 0.50; mark midpoint 0.375 = 3/8"],"workedExamples":[{"problem":"Find a rational number between 2/5 and 3/5","solution":"Mean = (2/5 + 3/5) ÷ 2 = 1/2 ÷ 2 = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4… wait — (1) ÷ 2 = 0.5 = 1/2. Correct: 1/2 lies between 0.4 and 0.6."}],"questions":[{"q":"Between which two integers does -7/4 lie?","expected":"Between -2 and -1."}],"differentiation":"Struggling students use decimal conversions; advanced students prove infinitude using p+q/2 recursively."},{"stage":"EXPLAIN","durationMinutes":12,"title":"Properties That Power Arithmetic","teacherScript":"Formally present closure, commutativity, associativity and the role of 0 and 1. Emphasise: rationals are closed under +, −, ×, ÷ (except ÷0). Write the property table and have students copy it.","analogy":"Commutativity is a two-door room: you enter from either side, you reach the same place.","boardWork":["Property table: a+b = b+a, a×b = b×a, (a+b)+c = a+(b+c)","Additive identity 0, multiplicative identity 1, reciprocal of a/b is b/a"],"workedExamples":[{"problem":"Verify: -3/7 + 5/6 = 5/6 + (-3/7)","solution":"LHS: (-18 + 35)/42 = 17/42. RHS: (35 - 18)/42 = 17/42. ✓ Equal."},{"problem":"Multiply: -2/9 × 3/4","solution":"= (-2×3)/(9×4) = -6/36 = -1/6."}],"questions":[{"q":"What is the additive inverse of -4/9?","expected":"4/9."},{"q":"Are rationals closed under division?","expected":"Yes, except division by zero."}],"differentiation":"Provide a printed property table to students with note-taking difficulties."},{"stage":"ELABORATE","durationMinutes":10,"title":"Chennai Market Math","teacherScript":"Students apply rationals to real contexts: currency exchange (1 USD = ₹84.10), temperature, and recipe scaling. Solve in pairs, then present one solution each.","analogy":"Exchange rates are rational numbers working overtime!","boardWork":["Exchange table: USD→INR, EUR→INR, AED→INR","1 USD = ₹84.10 · 1 EUR = ₹91.25 · 1 AED = ₹22.89"],"workedExamples":[{"problem":"Convert 2.5 USD to INR at 84.10","solution":"2.5 × 84.10 = ₹210.25. Both 2.5 and 210.25 are rationals."}],"questions":[{"q":"If 3 pizzas are shared by 4 friends, what rational describes each share?","expected":"3/4 pizza each."}],"differentiation":"Advanced: solve a two-step exchange problem through a third currency."},{"stage":"EVALUATE","durationMinutes":5,"title":"Exit Ticket — 3 Quick Ones","teacherScript":"Hand exit slips: (1) Write -2⅓ as p/q. (2) Insert one rational between 3/5 and 4/5. (3) True/False: subtraction of rationals is commutative. Review answers immediately; reteach inverse operations tomorrow if >30% slip.","analogy":"","boardWork":[],"workedExamples":[],"questions":[{"q":"-2⅓ as p/q?","expected":"-7/3."},{"q":"One rational between 3/5 and 4/5?","expected":"7/10 (or 0.65 etc.)."},{"q":"Is subtraction commutative?","expected":"False."}],"differentiation":"Oral exit option for students with writing fatigue."}],"homework":{"tasks":["NCERT Ex 1.1 Q1–Q8","Create a number-line poster placing 10 rationals","Challenge: find three rationals between -1/3 and -1/4"],"expectedOutput":"Notebook work + poster submitted next class"},"assessment":{"formativeChecks":["Exit ticket accuracy ≥ 2/3","Group presentation of market-math solution"],"evidence":"Exit slips collected and graded; common errors logged in Passport","adjustment":"If closure property is shaky, start next lesson with a 5-minute properties relay"},"sourceRefs":["NCERT Mathematics Grade 8, Chapter 1","CBSE 2026-27 syllabus (active)"]}

{"schemaVersion":"lesson-plan.v1","title":"Force, Pressure & The Friction Playground","learningObjectives":["Define force and describe its effects with everyday examples","Explain pressure = Force/Area and why sharp knives cut better","Identify factors affecting friction and suggest ways to reduce or increase it"],"successCriteria":["Students diagram at least 3 forces acting on a book on a table","Students calculate pressure given force and area in SI units","Students classify surfaces by expected friction"],"materials":["Spring balance","Wooden block + glass sheet + sandpaper","Balloons","Push pins"],"stages":[{"stage":"ENGAGE","durationMinutes":7,"title":"Why Do We Slip?","teacherScript":"Show two shoes: one smooth sole, one ribbed. Ask why the ribbed one is safer on tiles. Tease out 'grip' → today's word: friction.","analogy":"Friction is the invisible handbrake of the universe — sometimes a hero, sometimes a villain.","boardWork":["Word map: force → push/pull → friction"],"workedExamples":[],"questions":[{"q":"Name one hero-case and one villain-case of friction.","expected":"Hero: brakes stop a car. Villain: machine parts wearing out."}],"differentiation":"Let ESL students draw instead of describe."},{"stage":"EXPLORE","durationMinutes":12,"title":"Drag Race Lab","teacherScript":"Groups drag a wooden block with a spring balance across desk, glass and sandpaper. Record readings. Compare and infer factors affecting friction.","analogy":"Dragging a suitcase over airport carpet vs. marble floor.","boardWork":["Table: surface vs. spring-balance reading"],"workedExamples":[],"questions":[{"q":"Which surface showed maximum friction? Why?","expected":"Sandpaper — rough interlocking surfaces."}],"differentiation":"Pre-filled observation tables for support group."},{"stage":"EXPLAIN","durationMinutes":12,"title":"Pressure = Force ÷ Area","teacherScript":"Formalise force (SI unit newton), pressure (pascal) and friction. Derive P = F/A. Why do camels have wide feet? Why does a nail have a sharp tip?","analogy":"Standing on one foot vs. two — same weight, double the area, half the ouch.","boardWork":["P = F/A with units","Worked derivation: 200 N on 2 m² → 100 Pa"],"workedExamples":[{"problem":"A girl of weight 400 N stands on one foot of area 0.01 m². Pressure?","solution":"P = 400/0.01 = 40,000 Pa = 40 kPa."}],"questions":[{"q":"Why do shoulder bags have wide straps?","expected":"Larger area → less pressure on the shoulder."}],"differentiation":"Advanced: compare pressure in Pa vs N/cm²."},{"stage":"ELABORATE","durationMinutes":9,"title":"Design a Better Shoe","teacherScript":"Teams design a sole for: (a) an ice rink, (b) a desert trek, (c) a football pitch. Justify friction choices.","analogy":"Engineers fight friction in engines but buy friction in tyres.","boardWork":[],"workedExamples":[],"questions":[{"q":"How do we reduce friction in machines?","expected":"Lubricants, ball bearings, smoothing surfaces."}],"differentiation":"Sentence starters for the design justification."},{"stage":"EVALUATE","durationMinutes":5,"title":"One-Minute Paper","teacherScript":"Students write: the most surprising thing learned + one question they still have. Review papers; address top question immediately if time permits.","analogy":"","boardWork":[],"workedExamples":[],"questions":[{"q":"Unit of force?","expected":"Newton (N)."},{"q":"Friction always opposes…?","expected":"Relative motion between surfaces."}],"differentiation":"Verbal one-minute reflection allowed."}],"homework":{"tasks":["NCERT Ex 11.1–12.2 selected questions","Find 5 friction examples at home — classify helpful/harmful"],"expectedOutput":"Chart of 5 examples with classification"},"assessment":{"formativeChecks":["Spring-balance readings within ±0.5 N across group trials","One-minute paper insight quality"],"evidence":"Lab sheet + one-minute papers","adjustment":"If P=F/A confuses, run the balloon + pin demo again with numbers"},"sourceRefs":["NCERT Science Grade 8, Chapters 9 & 10","CBSE 2026-27 syllabus (active)"]}

{"schemaVersion":"lesson-plan.v1","title":"Light — Laws of Reflection Lab","learningObjectives":["State and verify the laws of reflection","Draw ray diagrams for plane mirrors","Explain lateral inversion with examples"],"successCriteria":["Students trace incident and reflected rays with correct angles","Students predict image position for a plane mirror"],"materials":["Plane mirrors","Laser pointers (Class-safe)","Protractors","Ray boxes"],"stages":[{"stage":"ENGAGE","durationMinutes":6,"title":"Mirror, Mirror","teacherScript":"Hold text to a mirror — why is it reversed left-right but not up-down? Collect hypotheses.","analogy":"A mirror is a very polite bouncer: light goes in, must leave at the same angle it arrived.","boardWork":["Normal, incident ray, reflected ray diagram"],"workedExamples":[],"questions":[{"q":"What is the 'normal'?","expected":"Perpendicular to the mirror surface at the point of incidence."}],"differentiation":"Provide labelled diagram handout."},{"stage":"EXPLORE","durationMinutes":14,"title":"Angle Hunt","teacherScript":"Groups shine rays at 20°, 45°, 60° and measure reflection angles. Tabulate i vs r.","analogy":"Billiards: the angle you hit the cushion is the angle it returns.","boardWork":["i vs r table"],"workedExamples":[],"questions":[{"q":"If i = 35°, r = ?","expected":"35° — laws of reflection."}],"differentiation":"Pre-set laser stations for support group."},{"stage":"EXPLAIN","durationMinutes":10,"title":"Two Laws, One Image","teacherScript":"Formalise: (1) i = r, (2) incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane. Image formation: virtual, erect, laterally inverted, same size, image distance = object distance.","analogy":"","boardWork":["Full ray diagram of image formation in plane mirror"],"workedExamples":[{"problem":"You stand 2 m from a mirror. Where is your image and how far from you?","solution":"Image is 2 m behind mirror; 4 m from you."}],"questions":[{"q":"Why is the image called virtual?","expected":"Rays only appear to come from it — no actual light converges there."}],"differentiation":"Peer diagram-checking protocol."},{"stage":"ELABORATE","durationMinutes":10,"title":"Ambulance Writing","teacherScript":"Why is AMBULANCE written in mirror script? Students sketch the mirror-word design for their own name.","analogy":"Lateral inversion flips your handshake: right hand meets left hand.","boardWork":[],"workedExamples":[],"questions":[{"q":"Is the image in a plane mirror magnified?","expected":"No — same size."}],"differentiation":"Advanced: periscope design bonus."},{"stage":"EVALUATE","durationMinutes":5,"title":"Ray-Diagram Relay","teacherScript":"Each row completes one step of a ray diagram on the board under time pressure. Grade for accuracy of angles and normals.","analogy":"","boardWork":[],"workedExamples":[],"questions":[{"q":"State both laws of reflection.","expected":"i = r; incident, reflected, normal coplanar."}],"differentiation":"Verbal law-statement option."}],"homework":{"tasks":["Draw ray diagrams: object at 3 cm, 5 cm from mirror","List 4 uses of plane mirrors at home"],"expectedOutput":"Diagram sheet with labels"},"assessment":{"formativeChecks":["i vs r tables consistent","Relay diagram accuracy"],"evidence":"Lab table + relay board photo","adjustment":"Redo laser demo with larger protractors if angles exceed ±3° error"},"sourceRefs":["NCERT Science Grade 8, Chapter 13","CBSE 2026-27 syllabus (active)"]}

{"instructions":"All questions are compulsory. Marks are shown against each question. Use of calculators is not permitted. Draw neat diagrams wherever necessary.","sections":[{"name":"Section A — Multiple Choice","type":"MCQ","marksEach":1,"questions":[{"q":"Which of the following is a rational number?","options":["π","√2","0.333… (repeating)","√5"],"answer":"C","chapter":"Rational Numbers","difficulty":"easy","cognitive":"Remember"},{"q":"The additive inverse of -7/13 is:","options":["7/13","-13/7","13/7","0"],"answer":"A","chapter":"Rational Numbers","difficulty":"easy","cognitive":"Remember"},{"q":"A square tile has area 144 cm². Its side is:","options":["12 cm","14 cm","24 cm","72 cm"],"answer":"A","chapter":"Squares and Square Roots","difficulty":"easy","cognitive":"Apply"},{"q":"The sum of interior angles of a quadrilateral is:","options":["180°","270°","360°","540°"],"answer":"C","chapter":"Understanding Quadrilaterals","difficulty":"easy","cognitive":"Remember"},{"q":"If 3(x - 2) = 15, then x =","options":["3","5","7","9"],"answer":"C","chapter":"Linear Equations in One Variable","difficulty":"easy","cognitive":"Apply"},{"q":"Which is a perfect cube?","options":["64","100","125","200"],"answer":"C","chapter":"Cubes and Cube Roots","difficulty":"medium","cognitive":"Understand","note":"64 and 125 are both cubes — corrected key: accept A or C"},{"q":"The multiplicative identity for rationals is:","options":["0","1","-1","1/2"],"answer":"B","chapter":"Rational Numbers","difficulty":"easy","cognitive":"Remember"},{"q":"Data: 4, 6, 8, 6, 6. The mode is:","options":["4","6","8","30"],"answer":"B","chapter":"Data Handling","difficulty":"easy","cognitive":"Apply"},{"q":"(a + b)² equals:","options":["a² + b²","a² + 2ab + b²","a² - 2ab + b²","2ab"],"answer":"B","chapter":"Algebraic Expressions and Identities","difficulty":"easy","cognitive":"Remember"},{"q":"1 kW h (unit of electricity) equals:","options":["3.6 × 10⁶ J","3.6 × 10³ J","1000 J","6 × 10⁵ J"],"answer":"A","chapter":"Chemical Effects of Electric Current","difficulty":"medium","cognitive":"Remember"}]},{"name":"Section B — Short Answer","type":"SA","marksEach":3,"questions":[{"q":"Represent -3/5 and 7/5 on a number line. Insert two rational numbers between them.","answer":"Diagram; e.g. -2/5 and 1/5 (any correct pair). 1 mark diagram, 2 marks insertions.","chapter":"Rational Numbers","difficulty":"medium","cognitive":"Understand"},{"q":"Solve: (2x - 1)/3 + (x + 2)/4 = 5. Show all steps.","answer":"Multiply by 12: 4(2x-1) + 3(x+2) = 60 → 8x - 4 + 3x + 6 = 60 → 11x = 58 → x = 58/11. Steps 2 marks, answer 1 mark.","chapter":"Linear Equations in One Variable","difficulty":"medium","cognitive":"Apply"},{"q":"The angles of a quadrilateral are in ratio 1:2:3:4. Find all angles.","answer":"x + 2x + 3x + 4x = 360 → 10x = 360 → x = 36°. Angles: 36°, 72°, 108°, 144°. Ratio setup 1, solve 1, answer 1.","chapter":"Understanding Quadrilaterals","difficulty":"medium","cognitive":"Apply"},{"q":"Find the smallest square number divisible by 8, 12 and 15.","answer":"LCM(8,12,15) = 120 = 2³×3×5. For a perfect square make exponents even: 2⁴×3²×5² = 3600. Method 2 marks, answer 1 mark.","chapter":"Squares and Square Roots","difficulty":"hard","cognitive":"Analyse"}]},{"name":"Section C — Long Answer","type":"LA","marksEach":5,"questions":[{"q":"A water tank is a cuboid of dimensions 2 m × 1.5 m × 1 m. (a) Find its capacity in litres. (b) If water costs ₹72.00 per 1000 L, find the cost to fill it.","answer":"(a) Volume = 3 m³ = 3000 L. (b) Cost = 3 × 72.00 = ₹216.00. Volume 2 marks, conversion 1, cost 2.","chapter":"Mensuration","difficulty":"hard","cognitive":"Apply"},{"q":"Verify the identity (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² for a = 3, b = -4, then use it to expand (2x + 5)².","answer":"LHS: (3-4)² = 1. RHS: 9 + 2(3)(-4) + 16 = 25 - 24 = 1 ✓. (2x+5)² = 4x² + 20x + 25. tables.name: Flashcard
rows: State the two laws of reflection.
1) Angle of incidence = angle of reflection. 2) Incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane.
The bending of light as it passes from one medium to another because its speed changes.
What kind of image does a plane mirror form?
Virtual, erect, laterally inverted and the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
n = speed of light in vacuum / speed of light in the medium (n = c / v).
Why does a pencil look bent in a glass of water?
Light from the submerged part refracts away from the normal as it leaves water, so the pencil appears raised and bent.
Which mirror is used in vehicle rear-view mirrors and why?
Convex mirror — it always forms an erect, diminished image and gives a wider field of view.
When light travels from denser to rarer medium at an angle greater than the critical angle, it is completely reflected back.
(x + 2)(x + 3) — two numbers that add to 5 and multiply to 6.
